head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: sum(c // mid for c in candies)
Number of children who can get `mid` candies each, if every pile is split into piles of size mid (leftovers are wasted)
Counting how many pieces of a size fit
Upper middle, because `lo = mid` keeps mid and must make progress
Binary search for the largest feasible value
0 candies each is always possible; more than the biggest pile never is

p: If every child can get x candies, they can also get x − 1, so feasibility is monotone and there is a largest feasible x. Each pile is split independently, so the count is just the sum of floors.

2226.takeaway: Binary search on candies per child; feasibility counts Σ floor(pile / size) ≥ k.

The '(' goes before position i of the left number (i = 0 means right at the start)
The ')' goes after j digits of the right number (at least 1, and up to all of them)

Value of the expression with those parentheses

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Post-order DFS (Depth-First Search) returning the subtree's sum and node count
Returning two numbers up the tree
Integer average (rounded down), compared to the node's value
The problem defines the average as the floor

blocks.h: Why compute sum and count together?
p: A node's average needs the totals of its whole subtree. Returning (sum, count) from the children lets each node combine them in O(1), so the whole tree is O(n); recomputing a subtree sum per node would be O(n²).

2265.takeaway: Post-order DFS returning (sum, count); compare floor(sum/count) with the node value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Monotonic stack of decreasing values; each value remembers how many rounds it survives before being removed
Elements on the stack that are ≤ x sit between x and the nearest larger element on its left; each of them is deleted (by a larger left neighbour) before x can be, so x pops them
x is removed after the longest chain of removals among the elements it 'absorbs'
If a larger element remains on the left, x will be deleted one step after the last of those finishes; if none, x never gets removed (0)

blocks.h: Why does a bigger-left element make x disappear?
p: Each round removes every element whose left neighbour is larger. x is removed once the elements between x and the nearest larger element on its left are gone and that larger element becomes its neighbour: the time is 1 + the longest removal time among the in-between elements. The stack stores exactly those removal times.

bullets: Time: O(n), each element pushed and popped once.

2289.takeaway: Monotonic stack where each element stores its removal round = 1 + the max round of the elements it covers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Weighted Union-Find (disjoint set): w[x] is the ratio x / parent[x]
Path compression that also multiplies weights, so afterwards w[x] = x / root
Already connected: the implied a / b is w[a] / w[b]; if it differs from v there is a contradiction (compare floats with a tolerance)
parent[ra] = rb; w[ra] = v * w[b] / w[a]
Union: set the weight so that a / b = v holds

bullets: Result: False (no contradiction): a/c implied by the first two equations is 3 × 0.5 = 1.5, and the given value is 1.5.

p: Each equation a / b = v links two variables with a ratio. Variables in one group have fixed ratios to the root, so any new equation between two group members can be checked in near-constant time against the stored ratios.

bullets: Time: near O(n α(n)) (α is the inverse Ackermann function).

2307.takeaway: Weighted Union-Find: store ratio to the root; a repeat connection must match the implied ratio within tolerance.

head: Code

p: `n = 7`, edges `[[0,2],[0,5],[2,4],[1,6],[5,4]]` give components of sizes 4, 2 and 1:

Each pair of nodes from different components should be counted exactly once. By removing the current component from `rest` first, `s * rest` counts pairs between it and the components processed after it; earlier components already counted their pairs with this one.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of strictly increasing paths that START at (i, j), including the single-cell path
DP (Dynamic Programming) on a grid with memoization
The path consisting of the cell alone
Extend to any strictly larger neighbour; because values strictly increase there are no cycles
Strict inequality makes the grid a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)

p: Each step goes to a strictly larger value, so the recursion can never return to a cell already on the current path. The grid with 'bigger neighbour' edges is acyclic, so the recursion depth is bounded and each cell is solved once.

bullets: Space: O(m·n) for the cache and recursion.

2328.takeaway: Memoized DFS counting increasing paths starting at each cell; strict increase prevents cycles.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Counts each distinct row; rows are lists, so they are converted to tuples to be hashable
Transposes: yields the columns as tuples
How many rows equal this column (a Counter returns 0 for unknown keys)

bullets: The column `(2, 7, 7)` equals the row `(2, 7, 7)`, the only matching pair, so the answer is 1.

blocks.h: Why counts and not a double loop?
p: Comparing every row with every column costs O(n³). Hashing the rows reduces each column check to O(n) for building its tuple plus an O(1) lookup, O(n²) in total. The Counter also handles duplicate rows: a column equal to two identical rows contributes 2.

2352.takeaway: Hash rows as tuples in a Counter and look up each column tuple.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum cost to be at the current stop having arrived by the regular route
Minimum cost to be at the current stop on the express route; it starts at `expressCost` because boarding costs once
To reach the next stop on the regular line you can come from either line (switching back to regular is free)
Stay on express, or pay the fee to switch from regular
Simultaneous update from the old values

blocks.h: Why compute both states each stop?
p: The cheapest way to reach a stop on the regular line may come from the express line (and vice versa), so both options must be kept: the best overall route to a later stop depends on which line you are on, not just on the cheapest total so far.

2361.takeaway: Two-state DP (regular vs express) with switching costs; answer each stop is the smaller.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: DFS (Depth-First Search) that adds an edge between every node and its parent in both directions, turning the tree into an undirected graph
Tree → graph so you can walk upward
BFS (Breadth-First Search) queue and visited set
Starts at −1 so the first layer (the start node itself) is minute 0
Processes one layer, i.e. one minute of spreading

p: Tree `[1,5,3,null,4,10,6,9,2]`, infection starts at node 3:
bullets: The last layer is at minute 4: the answer.

p: Infection spreads to children AND to the parent, but tree nodes have no parent pointer. Adding the parent edges makes the spread a plain BFS: the answer is the eccentricity (the greatest distance) from the start node.

2385.takeaway: Tree to undirected graph, then BFS from the start; the number of layers minus one is the time.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: sum(1 << j for j, v in enumerate(r) if v)
Each row becomes a bitmask of the columns where it has a 1
Row as a set of columns
From `itertools`: every way to choose numSelect columns
The row's 1s are a subset of the chosen columns: `~chosen` flips the bits, and AND with it leaves the 1s outside the selection (must be none)

p: Row masks (bit j = column j): `['000', '101', '110', '100']`. Choose 2 of 3 columns:
bullets: Best: 3 (the all-zero row is covered by any choice).

p: Covering a row means all its ones are inside the chosen set, a subset test that one AND does. Since n ≤ 12, trying all C(n, k) selections is cheap.

2397.takeaway: Rows as bitmasks; try every column combination and count rows whose mask is a subset.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A min-heap holding the end time of each group's last interval; `heap[0]` is the group that frees up first
The earliest-ending group finishes strictly before this interval starts (touching intervals overlap in this problem), so the interval can join it
Pops the smallest and pushes e in one step
Number of groups = most overlapping intervals at once

blocks.h: Why compare with the earliest ending group only?
p: If any group is free, the one that ends earliest is free. If even that group overlaps, all of them do, so a new group is required.

2406.takeaway: Sort by start and keep a min-heap of group end times; reuse the earliest-ending group when it has finished.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: XOR (exclusive or) of two consecutive prefix XORs cancels the common part and leaves arr[i]
The first element equals the first prefix

blocks.h: Why does this recover the array?
p: pref[i] = arr[0] ^ … ^ arr[i], and pref[i−1] = arr[0] ^ … ^ arr[i−1]. XOR-ing them cancels all the shared terms (x ^ x = 0), leaving arr[i].

2433.takeaway: arr[i] = pref[i] ^ pref[i−1] because XOR cancels the shared prefix.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Ceiling of total / (i + 1): the smallest possible maximum if the prefix sum could be spread evenly over i + 1 positions
The answer is the largest such bound over all prefixes, since moving value is only allowed to the left

p: An operation moves one unit from nums[i] to nums[i−1], i.e. leftwards. So the values in a prefix can never be lowered below its average, rounded up, but suffix values can flow into the prefix and never help it. The answer is the largest prefix average (rounded up).

2439.takeaway: Answer = max over prefixes of ceil(prefix sum / length), since values can only move left.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Pairs values with their per-unit cost and orders by value
Running total of weights; the first value where at least half of the total weight lies at or below it is the weighted median
Total cost of moving every value to the target

p: The total cost is a convex piecewise-linear function of the target; moving the target by 1 changes the cost by (weight on the left) − (weight on the right). The minimum is where the weight on each side first balances, which is the weighted median.

2448.takeaway: The optimal target is the weighted median of the values (weights = costs).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Difference between adjacent letters: the 'difference integer array' of the word
Group words by the same difference array
The odd word is alone in its group

p: `["adc","wzy","abc"]`:
bullets: `adc` and `wzy` share `(3, -1)`, while `abc` has `(1, 1)` and is alone in its group, so the answer is `abc`.

blocks.h: Why do the differences identify the odd word?
p: Words with the same difference array are shifted copies of each other. All but one word in the input share a difference array, so the one that stands alone in its group is the odd one.

2451.takeaway: Group words by their adjacent-letter difference tuple; the group of size one is the answer.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of strings of length exactly n that can be built by appending blocks of `zero` zeros or `one` ones
Counting DP (Dynamic Programming), like climbing stairs
The empty string is built in one way
The last block appended is a zero-block or a one-block
Total over all lengths in the allowed range

p: `low = 3, high = 3, zero = 1, one = 1`: each step appends '0' or '1', so dp doubles:

blocks.h: Why is this a stair-climbing DP?
p: A string of length n ends with a block of size `zero` or `one`, so the number of ways is the number of ways for the shorter string plus the other: the same shape as Climbing Stairs with steps `zero` and `one`.

2466.takeaway: Climbing-stairs DP with step sizes zero and one; sum dp over [low, high].
